fieldValues.title: 2. Two writers on one memory: the test
fieldValues.summary: Two people on separate clones can share one memory with today's tools: adds merge cleanly and a clash on one record is visible. A claimed author goes unchecked, and copying a split back silently lost an edit.
evidence: Build v0.1.0-build.602, dataModelRevision 11, a scratch repository with two git clones and ssh-signed commits, 2026-11-06.
10 notes each added concurrently to one container: git merge reported 0 conflicts, repo validate 0 errors, 21 members present.
Both writers edit one record: a git conflict in that one file, and repo validate fails until it is resolved.
SRS_ACTOR is self-declared: Bob created a note with createdBy alice and repo validate reported 0 errors.
An update by Bob left createdBy as alice and added no record of the editor.

A script comparing createdBy with the signer of the commit that added each file reported the forged record and no false positives on the honest clone. It needs git log --no-renames, because --follow treats near-identical JSON files as renames.
A relation to a record in another repository is refused with relation-endpoint-unknown.
slice export then archive unpack gave a new repositoryId, slice.origin.repositoryId and exportedAt, the same instance ids, and 0 validation errors. The origin holds no base version.
repo diff between home and split listed modified instances by id, with no way to say which side changed them.
Copying split records back over home discarded a home edit, with repo validate at 0 errors.
On srs-context origin/main, recent 'save: N files written through the server' commits have git signature status N (none), then a GitHub merge commit.
fieldValues.body:
Not tested: real agents, a shared server, a network, more than two writers, or long use. The clones avoid the registry server's lack of a write lock, which the 2026-11-04 research recorded.

The scratch repository was thrown away after the test. It is cheap to repeat.
